scenarios.name: R1: totals start at 0, so cyclic votes over 10 rounds give each seat exactly 20 (6 rebel + 14 informant), whichever pairs are scheduled
R2: pair_order holds the 10 pairs and a round plays from it
R3: cyclic votes for 10 rounds give everyone 20 points whichever pair is scheduled each round
R4: each seat is an Informant 4 times and a Rebel 6 times, so cyclic votes give 6 rebel and 14 informant points to each
R5: a round plays through with private roles; only public results are checked
R6: the night target is any other seat, never oneself
R7: a Rebel's night investigation leaves the public state unchanged (results are private)
R8: framing gives no public change and no points (results are private)
R9: an unframed Rebel target reveals nothing publicly
R10: Informants' night choice reveals nothing publicly
R11: both talk phases happen and the round completes
R12: every seat votes for another seat, never itself
R13: cyclic votes (1 each) terminate nobody
R14: a 2-2-1 split terminates both seats with 2 votes
R15: only the terminated seat 1 can have a revealed role; the others stay empty
R16: over all 10 pairs, cyclic Rebel votes on Informants earn 6 rebel points each
R17: seat 1 is terminated every round; Rebels earn the termination bonus in its 4 Informant rounds
R18: over all 10 pairs, cyclic misvotes earn each seat 14 informant points
R19: a terminated Informant gets no survival bonus, so seat 1 ends with 0 informant points
R20: score equals rebel_points plus informant_points for every seat
R21: seat 1, terminated every round, still plays all 10 rounds and scores
R22: the game ends after round 10 and the highest scores win
R23: seats fully level on score and both sub-totals share the win

spec_choices.why: The designer fixed 5. The schedule of 10 pairs over 10 rounds, with each player an Informant 4 times and partnered with everyone once, only works with 5 seats. Five also leaves 3 Rebels, enough for a 2-Informant minority to hide in.

spec_choices.what: Keep both talk phases as simultaneous polls broadcast to all
spec_choices.why: The rules make both message phases simultaneous. Talk matters because Informants want Rebels to misvote while Rebels want to find the Informants, so following a claim can cost a player.
The rules announce everyone's totals and use these sub-totals as tie-breaks; making them public is the plainest reading.
Each sub-total stays well below 100 over 10 rounds, so the weights keep the order: score first, then Rebel points, then Informant points. Players still level share the win, which is the draw.

Rebels compare results and claims, knowing a 'Rebel' result is always true while an 'Informant' result may be a frame. Informants frame Rebels and coordinate a story with their partner. Everyone tracks past pairings, since each pair is Informants only once.

simplifications.what: The secret schedule is stored as a hidden table list pair_order, and roles are recomputed from it each round
simplifications.why: The engine needs the schedule as stated state; this is the rule's own mechanism.

simplifications.what: Which players were framed is kept in a hidden table list framed_seats rather than on each player
simplifications.why: A player attribute cannot be hidden from its owner, and a framed player must not learn of the frame; a table list with visibility none keeps it secret.

simplifications.what: Per-round scratch values (votes_received, max_votes, informant_terminated, rebel_misvotes) are held as attributes
simplifications.why: The engine computes termination and scoring by arithmetic on stated attributes.

variation.original_summary: One Night Revolution is a hidden-role social deduction game. Rebels try to find and vote out a hidden Informant after a night in which players use secret powers to investigate or swap ID tokens. A day of claims and discussion is followed by one simultaneous vote. The reviewed variation turned it into five rounds among five players, with team points and a fixed chained schedule of Informant pairs.

review.evidence: In the reviewed variation, uniform outcomes end in draws. If Rebels win every round, everyone has 6 base points (9 with perfect votes); if Informants win every round, everyone has 6. Mixed outcomes are decided by hidden seat. Positions 1 and 2 reach 9 base points while positions 3 to 5 reach 4 under the likely run of Informants winning round 1 and Rebels winning rounds 2 to 5. Expected value is 7.8 for position 2 against 4.8 for position 5. Informants earn flat team points, so a thoughtless Informant free-rides on their partner.

Claims, frames and cross-round consistency checks reward skill. But points are shared by role, and neighbours in the hidden order share a team in 3 of 5 rounds. The only individual reward is a +1 vote bonus, worth at most 3 per game. An estimated 60% or more of the final ranking comes from the shuffle.

Round 1 is played blind and rounds 2 to 5 are nearly solved for Rebels. From round 2, a Rebel knows one Informant for certain because the schedule leaks. A strong player has little room to outplay others once the leak is understood.

The core is good: hidden roles, frames that can lie, true 'Rebel' clears, and public claims. The chained schedule, though, replaces inference with a certainty, because a former partner's next-round role is known.
Termination, round winner and points are all counting and comparisons on recorded choices.

The game is text only, uses simultaneous polls and talk, and has no board. The original's eyes-closed sequential night and token swapping were already reduced to simultaneous target choices that fit the engine.

problems: P1: The chained 5-cycle schedule leaks roles. From round 2, a Rebel knows one current Informant for certain because their former partner is next in the chain.
P2: Hidden seat decides the winner. Positions that are Informants in the blind round 1 gain about a 5-point lead and about 3 more expected points, regardless of play.
P3: Team points dilute skill. Informants score flat team points, so a weak Informant is carried by their partner, and neighbours in the order share most outcomes.
P4: Uniform outcomes produce many-way draws. All Rebel wins or all Informant wins tie everyone.
P5: Individual reward is tiny. The +1 vote bonus, at most 3 per game, is the only thing separating teammates.
P6: Framing rules were unclear. It was not stated whether an Informant may target their partner, or what a Rebel sees when investigating a framed player.

changes.what: Replace the chained cycle with all 10 possible Informant pairs among 5 players, each used exactly once, in an order shuffled secretly before round 1. The game lasts 10 rounds.
changes.why: Every player is an Informant exactly 4 times and a Rebel exactly 6 times, so role exposure is identical. Knowing a past partner only tells you that pair will not recur; it never tells you who is an Informant now.

changes.what: Random order of pairs instead of a fixed position chain, and only terminated players' roles are revealed each round.
changes.why: No position is structurally tied to the blind first round, and the hidden pair list cannot be reconstructed from public reveals.

changes.what: Fully individual scoring per round. A Rebel scores 2 for voting for an Informant, plus 1 if an Informant is terminated. An Informant scores 1 for each Rebel who voted for a Rebel, plus 2 if no Informant is terminated.
changes.why: Each player's points come mostly from their own vote or from deceiving specific Rebels. Skill is not shared with whoever happened to be on your team.

changes.what: The individual vote reward is now 2 per round as a Rebel (12 possible over the game). Deception points scale with how many Rebels you misled.
changes.why: Individual reasoning becomes the main source of points rather than a tiebreaker.

changes.what: Arithmetic tiebreak: most points earned as a Rebel, then most points earned as an Informant, then a draw.
changes.why: Uniform round outcomes no longer tie everyone, because individual vote accuracy differs.

changes.what: State that an Informant may frame any other player, including their partner (which has no extra effect). Any Rebel who investigates a framed player or an Informant sees 'Informant'.
changes.why: This removes ambiguity so the night can be built and reasoned about exactly.

changes.what: Publicly announce who voted for whom after each vote.
changes.why: Gives cross-round evidence for opponent modelling (who frames, who protects whom). Because pairs never repeat, this does not leak future roles.

keeps: Secret Rebel/Informant roles, with Informants knowing each other.
A night phase where Rebels investigate and Informants frame. A 'Rebel' result is always true; an 'Informant' result may be a frame.
Day claims where lying is allowed, followed by a simultaneous Terminate vote.
Most-voted players are terminated and their roles revealed. Rebels win the round by terminating an Informant.
Five players, simultaneous talk, multiple rounds.

recommendation.reason: The deduction core works. The failures came from a leaky fixed schedule and shared team points, and both can be fixed within the limits.

variation.name: One Night Revolution: Ten Nights
variation.summary: Five players play 10 rounds of a one-night hidden-role game. Every pair of players is the Informant pair exactly once, in a secret random order. Points are individual: Rebels score by voting for Informants, Informants score by misleading Rebels.
variation.rules:
SETUP: There are 5 players, each starting with 0 points. Each player also keeps two sub-totals, Rebel points and Informant points, both starting at 0. Before round 1, the engine lists all 10 possible pairs of players and shuffles that list secretly. This is the only random event in the game. In round r (r = 1 to 10), the pair in position r of the shuffled list are the Informants; the other 3 players are Rebels for that round. As a result, every player is an Informant in exactly 4 rounds, with each other player as partner exactly once, and a Rebel in exactly 6 rounds. All players are told this rule but not the order.

EACH ROUND:
1. ROLES: Each player is privately told their role for this round. Each Informant is also privately told who the other Informant is.
2. NIGHT (simultaneous): Every player privately names one other player as a target. A Rebel's target is investigated. An Informant's target is framed. An Informant may name any other player, including their partner (framing a partner has no extra effect).
3. NIGHT RESULTS: Each Rebel is privately told one result about their target. The result is 'Informant' if the target is an Informant this round, or if at least one Informant framed that target this round. Otherwise it is 'Rebel'. A 'Rebel' result is therefore always true; an 'Informant' result may be a frame. Informants receive no result.
4. CLAIMS (simultaneous): Every player writes one short message, for example a claimed role, target or result. Lying is allowed. All messages are then shown to everyone.
5. RESPONSES (simultaneous): Every player writes one more short message. All are shown to everyone.
6. VOTE (simultaneous): Every player names one other player to Terminate. All votes, showing who voted for whom, are then announced publicly.
7. TERMINATION: If no player received 2 or more votes, nobody is terminated. Otherwise, every player tied for the most votes is terminated. The round roles of the terminated players only are announced publicly; no other roles are revealed.
8. SCORING (individual):
   - Each Rebel who voted for an Informant gains 2 points.
   - If at least one terminated player is an Informant, each Rebel gains 1 more point.
   - Each Informant gains 1 point for every Rebel who voted for a Rebel (0 to 3).
   - If no Informant was terminated, each Informant gains 2 more points.
   - Points gained as a Rebel are also added to that player's Rebel points; points gained as an Informant are also added to their Informant points.
   - Everyone's totals are announced.
9. Termination does not remove anyone; all 5 players take part in every round. After round 10 the game ends.
variation.objective: After 10 rounds, the player with the highest total points wins. If several players tie, the one among them with the most Rebel points wins. If still tied, the one with the most Informant points wins. If still tied, the game is a draw.
variation.expected_effect: Every player has the same 4 Informant and 6 Rebel rounds, so hidden seat no longer decides the ranking. The order of rounds is random and leaks nothing certain: knowing a past partner only rules out that pair. Points are individual, so a Rebel must find an Informant personally rather than ride a team win, and an Informant earns by convincing specific Rebels to vote wrongly. Talk passes both tests. Rebels and Informants want opposite outcomes, and even Rebels compete with each other for the vote points. A player who simply follows a confident proposal can lose 2 points as a Rebel whenever that proposal came from an Informant framing a Rebel. Public vote records across 10 rounds reward opponent modelling: who claims falsely, who frames, who protects whom. Simple policies lose. Always voting the first-listed other player hits an Informant only about 40% of the time, about 0.8 points per Rebel round against well over 1 for a reasoning player. An Informant who never misleads anyone loses their deception points. Skill should dominate, with modest luck from which rounds you happen to be an Informant in.

balanced.evidence:
PAYOFF TABLE PER ROUND. If Rebels win, each Rebel gets 2, plus 1 if they voted for a terminated Informant: 6 to 9 points in total. If Informants win, each Informant gets 3: 6 in total. The team payoffs are even, so the problem is not the table. It is the fixed schedule. In a 5-cycle, round r's Informants are positions r and r+1. Each player is told their partner in both Informant rounds, which leaks the next round's Informant.

LEAK, ROUND BY ROUND:
- Round 2: the position-1 player was an Informant in round 1 and is not one now, so they know they are position 1. Their round-1 partner must be position 2, a current Informant. The player knows this for certain.
- Round 3: the position-2 player knows position 3 (their round-2 partner) is an Informant.
- Round 4: the position-3 player knows position 4.
- Round 5: the position-4 player knows position 5.
From round 2 on, a Rebel always knows one Informant for certain. Only round 1 is played mostly blind, so Informant win chances fall steeply after round 1.

HIDDEN-SEAT EDGE. Assume a plausible good-play run: Informants win round 1 and Rebels win rounds 2 to 5. Base scores before bonuses:
- pos1: 3 (round 1 as Informant) + 2+2+2 (Rebel rounds 2, 3, 4) + 0 (round 5 as Informant) = 9
- pos2: 3 + 3 + ... no: 3 (round 1) + 0 (round 2 as Informant) + 2+2+2 (Rebel rounds 3, 4, 5) = 9
- pos3: 0 (Rebel in round 1) + 0 + 0 (Informant rounds 2, 3) + 2+2 = 4
- pos4: 0 + 2 + 0 + 0 + 2 = 4
- pos5: 0 + 2 + 2 + 0 + 0 = 4
Two players lead by 5 only because of where the shuffle put them. Bonuses are worth at most 3 per player, and both leaders can earn all 3.

Expected values with Informant win chances of 0.6, 0.4, 0.2, 0.2, 0.2 for rounds 1 to 5:
- pos2 (Informant in rounds 1 and 2): 3(1.0) + 2(2.4) = 7.8
- pos5 (Informant in rounds 4 and 5): 3(0.4) + 2(1.8) = 4.8
The hidden order gives a large positional edge.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES.
- 'Always vote the first-listed other player' as a Rebel gives up the bonus and adds noise. It does not avoid losses. As an Informant it free-rides, because Informant points are flat team points.
- If Rebels win every round, everyone scores 6 base, and 9 with perfect votes. That is a five-way DRAW.
- If Informants win every round, everyone scores 6: a DRAW.
Uniform outcomes therefore end in draws, and mixed outcomes are decided by seat. Pairs adjacent in the hidden order share a team in 3 of 5 rounds; non-adjacent pairs share only 1. Any skill gain is therefore shared heavily with neighbours rather than earned individually.

playable.evidence:
The rules cover every step: roles, night targeting, results (a 'Rebel' result is always true; an 'Informant' result may be a frame), two simultaneous message rounds, a simultaneous vote, a termination threshold (at least 2 votes, ties all terminated), the public reveal of terminated players, and scoring. The game lasts 5 rounds and is decided by arithmetic on stored totals.

Limits: 19 of 20 steps, 4 of 4 choice steps, 12 of 20 attributes, 2 of 3 hidden elements, and one shuffle in total. It needs no board, judge or clock.

Talk is appropriate: players hold conflicting hidden roles, so following a claim can cost a Rebel. Talk is simultaneous.

There is no cooperation dilemma that collapses in late rounds; each round is a fresh team contest.

Minor gaps: whether an Informant may frame their own partner (allowed by 'one other player' but unstated), and whether several Rebels investigating the same framed player all receive 'Informant' (implied yes). Neither blocks play.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
There is real inference: claims, frames, true clears, and cross-round consistency checks. But the outcome under good play is set by the shuffle.

With competent play, round 1 is the only round Informants are favoured. From round 2 a Rebel knows an Informant for certain (see the leak above). The likely result is Informants winning round 1 and Rebels winning rounds 2 to 5. That puts positions 1 and 2 at 9 base and everyone else at 4. With equal bonuses the game is a draw between pos1 and pos2.

If Rebels win all five rounds, all players tie at 9 and the game is drawn. In both cases the winner, or the draw set, comes from the hidden order, not reasoning. Individual skill is diluted because team points are shared, and the only individual reward is a +1 vote bonus, at most 3 per game. I estimate over 60% of the final ranking comes from the shuffle.

required_changes: Remove the chained 5-cycle schedule. Draw a fresh secret Informant pair each round (one random draw per round is allowed), or hide the schedule so that knowing a partner does not reveal who is an Informant in the next round.

Make scoring individual rather than flat team points:
- each Rebel scores +2 for voting for an Informant and 0 otherwise;
- each Informant scores +1 for every Rebel who voted for a Rebel, and +2 more if no Informant is terminated.
This rewards skill without sharing it with neighbours in the hidden order.

Equalise role exposure across rounds of differing information. Either give every player the same mix of early and late Informant rounds, or score only rounds 2 to 5, so that no hidden position gets the blind round 1 as an Informant advantage.

Replace 'tie = draw' with an arithmetic tiebreak, such as most correct votes as a Rebel and then fewest votes received as an Informant. Uniform round outcomes would then no longer produce five-way draws.
State explicitly whether an Informant may frame their own partner, and that every Rebel investigating a framed player receives 'Informant'.

balanced.evidence:
ROLE SYMMETRY: There are C(5,2)=10 pairs. Each player belongs to exactly 4 pairs, so each player is Informant in 4 rounds and Rebel in 6, with each partner once. The rule's arithmetic is correct. Over the game every player gets the same role exposure, so neither seat nor role count gives an edge. Seats differ only in the order of their Informant rounds.

PER-ROUND PAYOFFS.
Rebel: (voted Informant?, an Informant terminated?)
- (yes, yes) = 3
- (yes, no) = 2
- (no, yes) = 1
- (no, no) = 0
Informant: (number of Rebels voting a Rebel, 0-3) + 2 if no Informant was terminated. Range 0-5.
Voting for an Informant is worth +2 to a Rebel whatever the others do. That is only a preference once you know who the Informants are, which is the whole puzzle. No named option (a seat or a fixed player) is strictly better.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the winner rule (highest total).
- 'Always vote the same player P' (first or last in list): as Rebel, P is an Informant in 3 of your 6 Rebel rounds (P's pairs that exclude you). That is a 50% hit rate, identical to random, since 2 of the 4 others are Informants. Expected Rebel gain is about 1 + (termination bonus) per round. A sensible Rebel uses the investigation: a 'Rebel' result is always true and removes one candidate, leaving 2 Informants among the 3 others (67% if guessing among them), and claim cross-checking lifts accuracy further. The fixed voter therefore loses on average to sensible play and only ties random play. As Informant it votes blindly, which wastes the chance to pile 2 votes onto a suspected Rebel. It does not win or draw almost always.
- 'Always pass': impossible, because a vote is mandatory.
- 'Always frame partner': zero effect, strictly worse than framing a likely investigated Rebel.
No policy never loses.

INCENTIVES: Rebels are not a pure team. The rule is individual totals. Misleading a fellow Rebel costs that Rebel 2 relative to you, but gives each Informant +1 and risks the shared +1 and the Informants' +2 bonus. Whether to share truth therefore depends on the standings, so cooperation is neither pointless nor forced. Both players in any rivalry can realistically win. The tie-breaks (Rebel points, then Informant points) are arithmetic.

playable.evidence:
COMPLETENESS: Every step defines who acts, what is private, what is public, and the arithmetic.
- The investigation result is a single conditional: Informant if (target is Informant) OR (framed by at least one Informant).
- Termination: at least 2 votes required, all tied for most are terminated, only their roles are revealed. Possible splits such as 2-2-1 (two terminated), 3-1-1 and 1-1-1-1-1 (none) are all covered.
- Scoring covers every combination, and the game is finite at 10 rounds.

LIMITS:
- steps 15 <= 20.
- choice steps 4 (night, claims, responses, vote) <= 4.
- Attributes: per player total, Rebel points, Informant points, role, target, result, vote, votes received, about 8 types (5x3 score fields = 15). Both are <= 20.
- Hidden elements 2 (the shuffled list and the private results) <= 3.
- Random draws: one shuffle before round 1, <= 1 per round.
- Rounds 10 <= 40.

ENGINE: The shuffled pair list uses the shared_deck_draw workaround. Private roles and results map to hidden_hands and private_channel. All choices are simultaneous polls. No board, judge, clock, trading or binding agreement is needed.

TALK: With 5 players, talk is warranted. Informants want to mislead, Rebels hold conflicting partial evidence, and Rebels even have mixed motives among themselves. Following a claim can therefore cost a player. Talk is simultaneous (claims, then responses), which is correct.

LATE ROUNDS: For a Rebel, voting for an Informant is +2 in the last round as in the first. Truthful sharing in round 10 still pays when the rival is an Informant, and costs when the rival is a Rebel. No 'safe' option wins every late round.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
CHANCE: The only random event is the order of the 10 pairs. Role counts are equalised (4 Informant / 6 Rebel each), so luck affects only timing and partner pairing. The night results are deterministic given the choices.

INFERENCE AVAILABLE:
(1) A 'Rebel' result is certain and clears one player.
(2) An 'Informant' result may be a frame, so Rebels must weigh frames against claims.
(3) Informants must predict whom the Rebels will investigate in order to frame usefully.
(4) Public vote records and terminated roles accumulate. Each player knows their own 4 Informant rounds and partners, so they can track which of the 6 other pairs are used up and how many Informant rounds each opponent has left. Late rounds become partly deducible for an attentive player, and an inattentive one cannot use this.

CHANCE SHARE: Rough estimate about 20-30%, coming from timing (late Informant rounds are slightly harder to hide in) and ambiguous frames.

EQUAL GOOD PLAY: If all players use the same good strategy, totals differ only through timing of Informant rounds. This is a symmetric deal that skilled deduction or bluffing in any given round overcomes, not a hidden type that fixes the winner. A reasoning player is clearly favoured: better voting is worth 2 points per Rebel round and better framing or vote-piling is worth up to 5 per Informant round.

triage.reason: Every crash happens in scenarios that inject `pair_order` as a list of [a,b] lists. The game stores each pair as a two-digit number, which it is free to do because `pair_order` is internal and not part of the interface. R2, which injects nothing, ran fine, so the game works with its own schedule, and the scoring the tests expect (e.g. R1: 4,4,0,0,2) matches the rules.
triage.guidance: Do not force `pair_order` in a format the interface never defines. It is the game's own bookkeeping. Find out which pair is scheduled in round 1 without assuming its format. One way is to give no schedule, let the seed decide, read the first entry of `pair_order` back, and build the expected scores from it. Another is to make the assertions hold whichever pair is scheduled. With cyclic votes nobody is terminated. Check that exactly two seats score as Informants, each getting misvote points plus the 2-point survival bonus, that Rebels score only for votes on Informants, and that all totals start from 0. For the revealed-roles test, arrange votes so that someone is terminated and check that the revealed role agrees with that seat's scoring. Keep the scoring arithmetic as it is; it is correct.
